items.question_text: A 46-year-old man attends a Darwin general practice for a repeat script. He mentions that his mother was Aboriginal. He has not had a health assessment. He is well, works, and has no chronic disease recorded. He identifies when asked. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Offer it only if she already has diabetes
Require a certificate of Aboriginality before any discussion
Offer a 715 health assessment. Eligibility is by self-identification
Decline it. Urban residence removes eligibility
Book it in 3 months because the interval is 6 months
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Offer a 715 health assessment. Eligibility is by self-identification

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 46-year-old man attends a Darwin general practice for a repeat script. He mentions that his mother was Aboriginal. He has not had a health assessment.

2. THE RULE
The MBS 715 health assessment is offered on self-identification as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, at least 9 months apart, to a non-admitted patient, never to a hospital inpatient.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Item 715 is for a patient of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent, based on self-identification, at any age, in the community. Appearance, city residence, and the absence of a chronic disease do not decide it. It cannot be claimed if the same assessment was done in the preceding 9 months.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Offer it only if she already has diabetes: The assessment is preventive, not limited to known disease.
B. Require a certificate of Aboriginality before any discussion: A certificate is not the Medicare test.
D. Decline it. Urban residence removes eligibility: There is no urban exclusion.
E. Book it in 3 months because the interval is 6 months: The claiming interval is 9 months, and she has never had one.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
The MBS 715 health assessment is offered on self-identification as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, at least 9 months apart, to a non-admitted patient, never to a hospital inpatient.

---

items.question_text: A 52-year-old Aboriginal woman asks for help with the cost of her PBS medicines. She has not been registered for Closing the Gap. She asks if she can register herself online. What is the most appropriate action?
options: He must already be on a concession card
He can self-register on the Services Australia app
A PBS prescriber or eligible Aboriginal Health Practitioner registers him once, after a clinical assessment
Registration is only available in remote clinics
Registration has to be repeated at every new pharmacy
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. A PBS prescriber or eligible Aboriginal Health Practitioner registers him once, after a clinical assessment

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
He needs a one-off clinical registration. He cannot sign himself up, and he does not need to live remotely.

2. THE RULE
Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief needs a one-off registration by a PBS prescriber or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner; writing CTG on a script (optional since July 2021) or asking a pharmacist does not create eligibility.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
CTG PBS registration is done once, for life, by a PBS prescriber or an eligible Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner, through HPOS. The patient cannot self-register. It is not limited to remote areas or to concession-card holders, and it follows him across pharmacies.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. He must already be on a concession card: A concession card changes what he pays. It is not the entry rule.
B. He can self-register on the Services Australia app: Patients cannot self-register.
D. Registration is only available in remote clinics: Location does not restrict it.
E. Registration has to be repeated at every new pharmacy: One registration follows him.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
CTG PBS registration is one-off, by a prescriber or eligible health practitioner.

---

items.question_text: A 12-year-old boy in a remote clinic had acute rheumatic fever last year and is on secondary prophylaxis. His benzathine dose is due. A locum suggests oral penicillin for a week because the clinic is busy. What is the most appropriate action?
options: One benzathine dose now, then review in 12 months
Give intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, no later than 28 days after the last dose
Stop prophylaxis because the acute illness has settled
Give daily erythromycin as the routine alternative
Oral amoxicillin for 5 days each month is first-line
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Give intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, no later than 28 days after the last dose

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
She needs benzathine benzylpenicillin on a 28-day clock. Oral amoxicillin for 5 days a month is not secondary prophylaxis.

2. THE RULE
RHD secondary prophylaxis is IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days (weight-adjusted dose), with duration set by disease severity and overdue doses given promptly.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin is first-line secondary prophylaxis, given no later than 28 days after the last dose. A 21-day interval is for breakthrough recurrence, not the routine start. Oral penicillin is less effective and is not the routine substitute. Erythromycin is for true penicillin hypersensitivity.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. One benzathine dose now, then review in 12 months: The interval is 28 days, not a year.
C. Stop prophylaxis because the acute illness has settled: The point of prophylaxis is to prevent the next episode.
D. Give daily erythromycin as the routine alternative: Macrolide is for hypersensitivity, which she does not have.
E. Oral amoxicillin for 5 days each month is first-line: Short oral courses are not secondary prophylaxis.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
First-line secondary prophylaxis is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin.

---

items.question_text: A 9-year-old in Townsville has fever, migratory arthritis, and a new murmur. You suspect acute rheumatic fever. A colleague says to wait for echocardiogram confirmation before notifying. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Notification is the family's responsibility
Wait for the 6-week echocardiogram
Notification is only required if he has severe carditis
Notify only if a household contact develops a sore throat
Notify now and link him to the RHD control program
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Notify now and link him to the RHD control program

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Definite acute rheumatic fever is notified now. The 6-week echocardiogram does not delay that.

2. THE RULE
Suspected acute rheumatic fever needs echocardiography, notification and referral to the RHD register.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Acute rheumatic fever is notifiable and the child should be registered with the jurisdictional RHD control program. The echocardiogram grades cardiac involvement. It does not gate the notification.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Notification is the family's responsibility: It is a clinician and public-health duty.
B. Wait for the 6-week echocardiogram: That loses the start of secondary prophylaxis and contact care.
C. Notification is only required if he has severe carditis: Severity changes prophylaxis duration, not whether he is notified.
D. Notify only if a household contact develops a sore throat: The case is notifiable regardless of contacts.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
ARF is notifiable on diagnosis.

---

items.question_text: A 15-year-old girl had acute rheumatic fever with moderate carditis three years ago. She has had no recurrence. Her mother asks if the benzathine can stop at five years for everyone. Moderate RHD means a longer course than a fixed five years. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop now because adherence has been perfect
Stop at 5 years because that is the universal rule
Duration is decided by the family, not the echocardiogram
Switch to oral penicillin for the remaining years
Continue according to the moderate-RHD duration, which is longer than the no-carditis rule
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Continue according to the moderate-RHD duration, which is longer than the no-carditis rule

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Moderate RHD does not stop at the no-carditis interval. His cousin's 5-year rule is the wrong line.

2. THE RULE
RHD secondary prophylaxis is IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days (weight-adjusted dose), with duration set by disease severity and overdue doses given promptly.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
No-carditis disease is a minimum of 5 years or until 21, whichever is longer. Moderate RHD is a minimum of 10 years after the last ARF or until 35, whichever is longer. His cousin's rule does not apply to his valve.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Stop now because adherence has been perfect: Adherence is why it works. It is not a reason to stop early.
B. Stop at 5 years because that is the universal rule: Five years is the no-carditis line.
C. Duration is decided by the family, not the echocardiogram: The family is part of the plan. The duration is clinical.
D. Switch to oral penicillin for the remaining years: Oral is not the routine remaining regimen.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Prophylaxis duration follows cardiac severity.

---

items.question_text: An 8-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community has infected skin sores and tea-coloured urine. A colleague treats the sores and says no further action is needed. Skin sores in a high-risk child are treated, and acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is looked for and notified where required. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give topical mupirocin only
Reassure the family and review the sores in 2 weeks
Assess and treat for acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and notify
APSGN does not follow skin infection, only pharyngitis
Start frusemide and send him home without bloods
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Assess and treat for acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and notify

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Puffy eyes, dark urine, and hypertension after skin sores is APSGN until proved otherwise. Do not wait 2 weeks.

2. THE RULE
Skin sores in a high-risk child are treated, APSGN is assessed and notified, and household contacts are examined for sores and scabies.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
In northern and remote Australia, APSGN usually follows group A streptococcal skin infection. Oedema, dark urine, and hypertension in a child with sores is APSGN until assessed otherwise. It is notifiable in several jurisdictions and needs same-day clinical care, not a 2-week wait.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Give topical mupirocin only: Topical care does not treat APSGN.
B. Reassure the family and review the sores in 2 weeks: The renal signs are the emergency, not the crusts alone.
D. APSGN does not follow skin infection, only pharyngitis: In this setting skin is the usual source.
E. Start frusemide and send him home without bloods: He needs assessment, not an unmonitored diuretic.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
APSGN in remote Australia usually follows skin infection.

---

items.question_text: A 55-year-old man from a Strongyloides-endemic northern community is about to start prednisolone for a flare of asthma. A colleague says to start the steroid and check serology later if he gets abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ivermectin is contraindicated if he has ever lived remotely
Start prednisolone. A normal eosinophil count excludes Strongyloides
Strongyloides is only a risk in returned travellers
Stool microscopy alone is sensitive enough to clear him
Check Strongyloides serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin before immunosuppression
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Check Strongyloides serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin before immunosuppression

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A normal eosinophil count does not clear Strongyloides. Screen or give ivermectin before the steroids.

2. THE RULE
Before corticosteroids or immunosuppression in a person from a Strongyloides-endemic setting, check serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Strongyloides is endemic in many remote northern communities. A normal eosinophil count does not exclude it, and stool microscopy is insensitive. Before immunosuppression he needs serology or pre-emptive ivermectin, because disseminated disease on steroids is dangerous.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Ivermectin is contraindicated if he has ever lived remotely: Remote residence is the reason to consider it.
B. Start prednisolone. A normal eosinophil count excludes Strongyloides: Eosinophilia is often absent.
C. Strongyloides is only a risk in returned travellers: Northern Australian communities are endemic.
D. Stool microscopy alone is sensitive enough to clear him: Stool microscopy misses most infections.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Strongyloides is endemic in remote northern Australia.

---

items.question_text: A 48-year-old man in Darwin presents in the wet season with severe pneumonia and sepsis. He works outdoors. He is deteriorating. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Add gentamicin for northern Australian sepsis
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is sufficient intensive therapy
Change to intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem and discuss melioidosis
Wait for culture before changing antibiotics
Ceftriaxone covers melioidosis, so continue it
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Change to intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem and discuss melioidosis

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Wet-season pneumonia and shock in a diabetic man in Darwin is melioidosis until proved otherwise. Use ceftazidime or meropenem.

2. THE RULE
Suspected melioidosis in tropical northern Australia is treated with IV ceftazidime or meropenem, not standard community pneumonia antibiotics.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Burkholderia pseudomallei is endemic in northern Australia, peaks in the wet season, and prefers people with diabetes. It is resistant to ceftriaxone and gentamicin. Intensive therapy is intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem. Waiting for culture in septic shock is the wrong delay.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Add gentamicin for northern Australian sepsis: The organism is intrinsically resistant to gentamicin.
B. Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is sufficient intensive therapy: Oral therapy is the eradication phase, not the septic start.
D. Wait for culture before changing antibiotics: Septic shock in this setting is treated on suspicion.
E. Ceftriaxone covers melioidosis, so continue it: It does not.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Melioidosis peaks in the northern wet season and in people with diabetes.

---

items.question_text: A 34-year-old woman attends a city practice. The receptionist has marked her as non-Indigenous based on appearance. She has not been asked. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Only ask if the patient raises culture first
Decide from skin colour
Record Aboriginal because the clinic is near an Aboriginal service
Ask the patient, in private, whether they identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander
Leave it blank. Asking is offensive
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Ask the patient, in private, whether they identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Ask everyone, in private. Do not infer status from a surname, a suburb, or skin colour.

2. THE RULE
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status is recorded from the person's own answer to the standard question, asked of every patient, and never assumed from appearance or required to be proven.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Identification is by asking the person, not by appearance, surname, or suburb. The question is asked of everyone, privately, because it changes preventive care, Medicare items, and PBS access. Leaving it blank loses that care.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Only ask if the patient raises culture first: The clinic asks. It does not wait.
B. Decide from skin colour: Appearance is not the test.
C. Record Aboriginal because the clinic is near an Aboriginal service: Proximity is not identity.
E. Leave it blank. Asking is offensive: Not asking is the error.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Indigenous status is self-identified.

---

items.question_text: A 24-year-old pregnant woman with known rheumatic heart disease is booked for routine low-risk antenatal care at the local clinic. She has moderate mitral stenosis. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Stop benzathine penicillin in pregnancy
Refer for specialist obstetric and cardiac care and restart secondary prophylaxis
Deliver at the local clinic because transfer is disruptive
Routine shared care is enough because she feels well
RHD is not a pregnancy risk if the last echo was normal 3 years ago
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Refer for specialist obstetric and cardiac care and restart secondary prophylaxis

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Moderate RHD in pregnancy needs specialist care and continuous benzathine prophylaxis. Feeling well is not the clearance.

2. THE RULE
A pregnant woman with known RHD needs shared specialist obstetric and cardiac care and continued secondary prophylaxis, not routine low-risk care.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Pregnancy increases cardiac demand, and moderate RHD needs specialist planning, including place of birth. Missed benzathine doses should be restarted. Feeling well does not downgrade the risk, and a 3-year-old echo is not current.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Stop benzathine penicillin in pregnancy: Secondary prophylaxis continues in pregnancy.
C. Deliver at the local clinic because transfer is disruptive: Place of birth is a specialist decision.
D. Routine shared care is enough because she feels well: Symptoms lag behind risk.
E. RHD is not a pregnancy risk if the last echo was normal 3 years ago: Three years is not a current assessment.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Pregnancy is a high-risk setting for RHD.

---

items.question_text: A child in a remote household has scabies and impetigo. The clinic has one tube of permethrin and the nurse plans to treat only the index child. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Oral ivermectin for the 4-year-old is always first-line
Antibiotics without scabies treatment will clear both
Scabies does not drive streptococcal skin infection
Treat the whole household for scabies and treat the impetigo
Treat only the index child
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Treat the whole household for scabies and treat the impetigo

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Treat the household for scabies and treat the sores. One tube for one child leaves the source in the house.

2. THE RULE
Scabies is treated in the whole household at the same time, with impetigo treated alongside, not just the index child.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Scabies is a household problem, and the breaks in the skin drive streptococcal impetigo, APSGN, and rheumatic fever. Contacts are treated at the same time. One index child is not the unit of treatment.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Oral ivermectin for the 4-year-old is always first-line: Weight, age, and pregnancy rules apply. It is not automatically first for every child.
B. Antibiotics without scabies treatment will clear both: The scabies remains.
C. Scabies does not drive streptococcal skin infection: It does, by breaking the skin.
E. Treat only the index child: Untreated siblings reinfect her.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Scabies is treated as a household.

---

items.question_text: A 40-year-old Aboriginal man is brought in drowsy and febrile. A colleague attributes it to alcohol because of his background and plans observation only. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Assess for serious infection, including meningitis, now
Leave him in the corridor. The smell of alcohol is the diagnosis
Confusion plus alcohol means no lumbar puncture is ever needed
A fever in an Aboriginal man is always pneumonia
Discharge when he is sober
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Assess for serious infection, including meningitis, now

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Fever, confusion, and neck stiffness are assessed now. The smell of alcohol is not the diagnosis.

2. THE RULE
Culturally safe care follows the patient's wishes about family and Aboriginal Health Workers but never replaces or delays clinical assessment, and symptoms are not attributed to stereotypes.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
The smell of alcohol is a finding, not a diagnosis. Fever, confusion, and neck stiffness need immediate assessment for meningitis and other sepsis. Ethnicity does not choose the diagnosis.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Leave him in the corridor. The smell of alcohol is the diagnosis: This is the stereotype trap.
C. Confusion plus alcohol means no lumbar puncture is ever needed: Alcohol does not forbid the investigation he may need.
D. A fever in an Aboriginal man is always pneumonia: That is another stereotype.
E. Discharge when he is sober: Sobriety does not treat meningitis.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Do not let ethnicity or the smell of alcohol close the differential.

---

items.question_text: A child in a trachoma-endemic community has active trachoma. A colleague gives one set of drops to the child and discharges him. What is the most appropriate action?
options: A normal vision test today means no treatment
Use the SAFE strategy: surgery where needed, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, and environmental improvement
Trachoma is viral and needs no antibiotics
One bottle for the index child is the program
Only adults are treated
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Use the SAFE strategy: surgery where needed, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, and environmental improvement

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Active trachoma is a community problem. Use SAFE, not one bottle for one child.

2. THE RULE
Trachoma in an endemic community is managed with the SAFE strategy (surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, environmental improvement).

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Trachoma control is the SAFE strategy: surgery for trichiasis, antibiotics for active infection, facial cleanliness, and environmental change. One bottle for one child leaves the household and the community untreated. Vision can be normal while follicles are active.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. A normal vision test today means no treatment: Follicles precede visual loss.
C. Trachoma is viral and needs no antibiotics: It is chlamydial.
D. One bottle for the index child is the program: That is not SAFE.
E. Only adults are treated: Active disease is in children.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
SAFE is surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, environment.

---

items.question_text: An Aboriginal Health Worker is in the room for a consultation. A junior doctor stops examining the patient and lets the worker take the history alone. What is the most appropriate action?

Ask the worker to diagnose the lump
Include the worker if the patient wants her, and still assess the lump
Exclude the worker. Medical discussions are doctor-only
Record that the patient refused care
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Include the worker if the patient wants her, and still assess the lump

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
If she wants her Aboriginal Health Worker present, include the worker and still assess the lump.

2. THE RULE
Culturally safe care follows the patient's wishes about family and Aboriginal Health Workers but never replaces or delays clinical assessment, and symptoms are not attributed to stereotypes.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
The patient chooses her support. An Aboriginal Health Worker improves communication and cultural safety. The doctor still examines and refers. Presence of the worker is not a refusal of care and not a transfer of diagnosis.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Cancel the consult because a worker is present: There is no reason to cancel.
B. Ask the worker to diagnose the lump: The worker supports. The doctor diagnoses.
D. Exclude the worker. Medical discussions are doctor-only: That removes a support the patient asked for.
E. Record that the patient refused care: She has not refused care.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
The patient chooses her support person.

---

items.question_text: A 14-year-old on benzathine secondary prophylaxis misses a dose by 10 days. A colleague restarts the whole course from zero and offers a short oral penicillin instead. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give the overdue benzathine dose now and reset the 28-day clock
Replace the missed dose with 5 days of amoxicillin
Stop prophylaxis. A missed dose ends the program
He must restart a 10-year course from today
Ceremony is a contraindication to further injections
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Give the overdue benzathine dose now and reset the 28-day clock

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Give the late benzathine dose now and restart the 28-day interval. Do not abandon the program.

2. THE RULE
RHD secondary prophylaxis is IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days (weight-adjusted dose), with duration set by disease severity and overdue doses given promptly.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
A late dose is given when he returns, and the next dose is 28 days from that injection. Ceremony is not a contraindication. A short oral course does not replace the injection, and one missed dose does not end the program.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Replace the missed dose with 5 days of amoxicillin: Oral catch-up is not the regimen.
C. Stop prophylaxis. A missed dose ends the program: Missed doses are recovered, not used to exit.
D. He must restart a 10-year course from today: The duration counts from the last ARF, not from one late dose.
E. Ceremony is a contraindication to further injections: Absence for ceremony is a reason to plan the next dose, not to stop.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A late dose is given on return.

---

items.question_text: A child is diagnosed with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The family has several children at home. Treating only the index child is incomplete. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Only the mother needs a throat swab
No contact action. APSGN is not transmissible
Exclude the whole community from school for a month
Give the household a single dose of ceftriaxone
Ask the clinic to examine household children for sores, scabies, and signs of APSGN
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Ask the clinic to examine household children for sores, scabies, and signs of APSGN

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Tell the clinic to check the other children for sores, scabies, and APSGN. The streptococcus is the transmissible part.

2. THE RULE
Skin sores in a high-risk child are treated, APSGN is assessed and notified, and household contacts are examined for sores and scabies.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
The streptococcus is transmissible. Household children need examination for sores, scabies, and early APSGN, and treatment of what is found. A month-long community exclusion and a household ceftriaxone dose are not the program.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Only the mother needs a throat swab: Skin, not only the mother's throat, is the usual source.
B. No contact action. APSGN is not transmissible: The immune disease is not caught. The streptococcus is.
C. Exclude the whole community from school for a month: Exclusion is for active sores until treated, not a community shutdown.
D. Give the household a single dose of ceftriaxone: That is not the contact regimen.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
APSGN itself is immune-mediated. The streptococcus is what spreads.

---

items.question_text: An Aboriginal man is an inpatient for pneumonia. A junior doctor wants to claim a 715 health assessment before discharge because he is in the building. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Only a specialist can do a 715
The assessment requires a certificate of Aboriginality
A 715 is not claimed for a hospital inpatient. Offer it after discharge
Inpatients are the only group eligible
Do the 715 on the ward. Admission is a good opportunity
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. A 715 is not claimed for a hospital inpatient. Offer it after discharge

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Do not claim a 715 on the ward. Offer it in the community after discharge.

2. THE RULE
The MBS 715 health assessment is offered on self-identification as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, at least 9 months apart, to a non-admitted patient, never to a hospital inpatient.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Item 715 is a general-practice assessment in consulting rooms or a place other than a hospital or residential aged care. An inpatient is not eligible. The preventive assessment can be offered after discharge.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Only a specialist can do a 715: It is a GP item.
B. The assessment requires a certificate of Aboriginality: Self-identification is enough.
D. Inpatients are the only group eligible: Inpatients are excluded.
E. Do the 715 on the ward. Admission is a good opportunity: The item excludes inpatients.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Item 715 excludes hospital inpatients and residential aged-care recipients.

---

items.question_text: A 7-year-old weighing 18 kg is due for benzathine secondary prophylaxis. A nurse draws up the adult dose of 1.2 million units. A child under 20 kg does not automatically get the adult dose. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give half the adult dose orally
Delay prophylaxis until she weighs 20 kg
Dose is chosen by age alone, ignoring weight
Give 600,000 units. Children under 20 kg receive the lower dose
Give 1,200,000 units. All children get the adult dose
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Give 600,000 units. Children under 20 kg receive the lower dose

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
At 18 kg she receives 600,000 units, not the adult 1,200,000-unit dose.

2. THE RULE
RHD secondary prophylaxis is IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days (weight-adjusted dose), with duration set by disease severity and overdue doses given promptly.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Children under 20 kg receive 600,000 units of benzathine benzylpenicillin. At 18 kg she is under that line. Waiting until 20 kg leaves her unprotected, and an oral half-dose is not the regimen.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Give half the adult dose orally: Route and dose are both wrong.
B. Delay prophylaxis until she weighs 20 kg: She needs prophylaxis now, at the correct dose.
C. Dose is chosen by age alone, ignoring weight: Weight is the split.
E. Give 1,200,000 units. All children get the adult dose: The adult dose is for 20 kg and over.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Under 20 kg: 600,000 units. At or over 20 kg: 1,200,000 units.

---

items.question_text: A 715 health assessment finds new hypertension and likely diabetes. The doctor completes the form and says follow-up is optional. What is the most appropriate action?
options: A single health check replaces a GP management plan
Repeat the 715 next week
The report completes the program
Arrange follow-up for the blood pressure and diabetes, including chronic-disease care
Diabetes found on a 715 is not treated until the next year
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Arrange follow-up for the blood pressure and diabetes, including chronic-disease care

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Book the follow-up. A 715 that finds diabetes and hypertension is the start of care, not the end.

2. THE RULE
Problems found at a 715 health assessment need an arranged follow-up plan, using post-assessment nurse/Aboriginal Health Practitioner and allied health follow-up items, not the next health check.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
The 715 finds the problem. Follow-up treats it. She needs blood-pressure care, diabetes care, and a plan. The item cannot be repeated within 9 months, and a report alone is not management.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. A single health check replaces a GP management plan: It can lead to one. It does not replace it.
B. Repeat the 715 next week: The claiming interval is 9 months.
C. The report completes the program: Finding disease without follow-up wastes the assessment.
E. Diabetes found on a 715 is not treated until the next year: It is treated now.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
The value of a 715 is the follow-up.

---

items.question_text: A child in a high-risk community has a streptococcal sore throat. A colleague says to watch it because primary prevention is surveillance. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give topical throat spray only
Treat the streptococcal sore throat now
Watch for 5 days. Antibiotics are not used for sore throats
Sore throats are irrelevant to rheumatic fever
Arrange echocardiography instead of antibiotics
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Treat the streptococcal sore throat now

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Treat the sore throat now. In this setting, watchful waiting is a missed chance to prevent rheumatic fever.

2. THE RULE
In populations at high risk of rheumatic fever, sore throats (ages 3-35) and skin sores are treated promptly as streptococcal, e.g. IM benzathine benzylpenicillin G or 10 days of amoxicillin, without waiting for swab results.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
In a high-risk child, a streptococcal sore throat is treated to prevent acute rheumatic fever. Waiting 5 days for spontaneous recovery is the missed primary-prevention step. Echo does not treat the infection.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Give topical throat spray only: Topical care does not clear group A streptococcus.
C. Watch for 5 days. Antibiotics are not used for sore throats: That rule does not apply in this risk setting.
D. Sore throats are irrelevant to rheumatic fever: They are a classic trigger.
E. Arrange echocardiography instead of antibiotics: Echo looks for carditis. It does not treat the throat.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Primary prevention is treatment of group A streptococcal infection.

---

Culturally safe care follows the patient's wishes about family and Aboriginal Health Workers but never replaces or delays clinical assessment, and symptoms are not attributed to stereotypes.

Cultural safety shapes communication. It does not withhold emergency care.

items.question_text: An Aboriginal woman with type 2 diabetes asks the pharmacist whether he can register her for Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief while he dispenses her script. Which of the following is most accurate?
options: She must re-register every script
Any staff member can tick CTG
CTG is only for remote patients
The pharmacist can register her at the counter
Registration is a one-off clinical step by a prescriber or eligible practitioner
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Registration is a one-off clinical step by a prescriber or eligible practitioner

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
An Aboriginal woman with type 2 diabetes asks the pharmacist whether he can register her for Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief while he dispenses her script.

2. THE RULE
Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief needs a one-off registration by a PBS prescriber or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner; writing CTG on a script (optional since July 2021) or asking a pharmacist does not create eligibility.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
CTG registration is clinical. The patient cannot self-register and the pharmacy cannot create it.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. She must re-register every script: Registration is one-off, not per script.
B. Any staff member can tick CTG: Only an eligible prescriber or Aboriginal Health Practitioner can register.
C. CTG is only for remote patients: CTG is available nationally, not only to remote patients.
D. The pharmacist can register her at the counter: Pharmacists do not create CTG registration.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief needs a one-off registration by a PBS prescriber or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner; writing CTG on a script (optional since July 2021) or asking a pharmacist does not create eligibility.

---

items.question_text: A 29-year-old man with fair skin and red hair registers at a Brisbane general practice and ticks 'Aboriginal' on the new-patient form. The practice nurse is unsure. Before booking the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health assessment (MBS item 715), she suggests recording him as non-Indigenous until he brings a confirmation of Aboriginality letter from a community organisation. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Record him as Aboriginal, as he identified, and offer the 715 health assessment
Record him as Aboriginal but defer the 715 until Services Australia confirms his eligibility
Record his status as 'not stated' because his answer and appearance do not match
Record him as non-Indigenous until he produces a confirmation of Aboriginality letter
Ask a family member to confirm his identity before changing the record
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Record him as Aboriginal, as he identified, and offer the 715 health assessment

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A patient has self-identified as Aboriginal on the registration form. A staff member wants documentary proof before recording his status or offering a 715 health assessment.

2. THE RULE
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status is recorded from the person's own answer to the standard question, asked of every patient, and never assumed from appearance or required to be proven.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
In clinical records and for MBS health assessments, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status is whatever the patient says in answer to the standard question. Appearance is irrelevant. Clinical care and Medicare eligibility for the 715 rest on self-identification, so no confirmation letter is needed. Asking for proof is a barrier to care and is culturally unsafe.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Record him as Aboriginal but defer the 715 until Services Australia confirms his eligibility: Services Australia does not pre-approve Indigenous status for a 715. Self-identification is enough.
C. Record his status as 'not stated' because his answer and appearance do not match: 'Not stated' is used only when the person has not been asked or chooses not to answer. He has answered.
D. Record him as non-Indigenous until he produces a confirmation of Aboriginality letter: Confirmation of Aboriginality letters are used for some employment and program purposes. Clinical records and the 715 use self-identification.
E. Ask a family member to confirm his identity before changing the record: A relative does not decide another adult's identity. His own answer is what gets recorded.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Record Indigenous status from the patient's own answer, without proof, and act on it.

---

items.question_text: An audit of a regional emergency department finds that Indigenous status is missing for 30% of presentations. The clerks explain that they ask the question only of patients who 'look Aboriginal', so that other patients are not offended. The department asks for one change to its registration process. What is the most appropriate change?
options: Ask the question only at inpatient admission, not in the emergency department
Continue asking only patients who appear to be Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander
Record status from the accompanying family member's answer by default
Infer status from the patient's postcode and surname to fill the gaps
Ask every patient the standard question about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander origin and record the answer as given
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Ask every patient the standard question about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander origin and record the answer as given

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A department asks some patients about Indigenous status based on appearance, and the data are incomplete.

2. THE RULE
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status is recorded from the person's own answer to the standard question, asked of every patient, and never assumed from appearance or required to be proven.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
National best-practice guidance (AIHW) is to ask every patient the standard question, 'Are you of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin?', and to record the answer as given. Selective asking based on appearance both under-identifies patients and stereotypes them. Without identification, patients miss targeted care such as the 715 health assessment, Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief and First Nations funded vaccines.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Ask the question only at inpatient admission, not in the emergency department: Deferring the question to admission leaves most emergency patients unidentified.
B. Continue asking only patients who appear to be Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander: Asking only by appearance is the cause of the missing data, and it stereotypes patients.
C. Record status from the accompanying family member's answer by default: An adult with capacity answers for themselves. A family member answers only when the patient cannot.
D. Infer status from the patient's postcode and surname to fill the gaps: Postcode and surname do not tell you identity. Status must come from the person.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Ask everyone the standard Indigenous status question and record the answer as given.

items.question_text: A 9-year-old Aboriginal girl in a remote Northern Territory community has had a sore throat and fever for 2 days. She has no cough, her tonsils are enlarged, and she has tender anterior cervical nodes. A throat swab is taken, but the result will take 4 days to come back. She has no history of rheumatic fever. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Wait for the swab result and treat only if group A streptococcus grows
Give oral amoxicillin for 3 days
Give a single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin G now (or 10 days of oral amoxicillin) without waiting for the swab
Order an echocardiogram before deciding on antibiotics
Give symptomatic treatment only, because most sore throats are viral
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Give a single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin G now (or 10 days of oral amoxicillin) without waiting for the swab

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A child in a population at high risk of acute rheumatic fever has a sore throat. The swab result is delayed.

2. THE RULE
In populations at high risk of rheumatic fever, sore throats (ages 3-35) and skin sores are treated promptly as streptococcal, e.g. IM benzathine benzylpenicillin G or 10 days of amoxicillin, without waiting for swab results.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
In populations at high risk of acute rheumatic fever, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 3 to 35 in remote northern Australia, a sore throat is treated as presumed group A streptococcus without waiting for the swab. The treatment is a single IM dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin G or 10 days of oral amoxicillin (2020 Australian ARF/RHD guideline). Treating promptly prevents ARF.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Wait for the swab result and treat only if group A streptococcus grows: Waiting 4 days delays primary prevention in a high-risk child. Treatment is started straight away.
B. Give oral amoxicillin for 3 days: Three days is too short to eradicate group A streptococcus. The oral course is 10 days.
D. Order an echocardiogram before deciding on antibiotics: Echocardiography is for suspected ARF or RHD. It is not a precondition for treating pharyngitis.
E. Give symptomatic treatment only, because most sore throats are viral: In high-risk settings sore throats are not managed as presumed viral.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
High-risk child with sore throat: treat for GAS now with IM benzathine (or 10 days of amoxicillin).

---

Paracetamol and review, because primary prevention applies only to children
Take a throat swab and treat only if it is positive
Refer her for echocardiography instead of treatment
Treat her for presumed group A streptococcal pharyngitis with IM benzathine benzylpenicillin G or 10 days of oral amoxicillin

An adult in a high-risk community has a sore throat, and the plan is to withhold antibiotics because of her age.

In populations at high risk of rheumatic fever, sore throats (ages 3-35) and skin sores are treated promptly as streptococcal, e.g. IM benzathine benzylpenicillin G or 10 days of amoxicillin, without waiting for swab results.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
The Australian ARF/RHD guideline recommends treating sore throats empirically in people aged 3 to 35 years from high-risk populations. ARF can occur in young adults as well as children. A 27-year-old in a high-incidence community is within the target group and should be treated now.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Treat only if she develops joint pain: Joint pain may already be ARF. Waiting for it is waiting for the disease you are trying to prevent.
B. Paracetamol and review, because primary prevention applies only to children: Primary prevention in high-risk settings covers people aged 3 to 35, not just children.
C. Take a throat swab and treat only if it is positive: A swab can be taken, but treatment should not wait for the result in a high-risk setting.
D. Refer her for echocardiography instead of treatment: Echocardiography does not prevent ARF. Treating the streptococcal infection does.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY

items.question_text: A 34-year-old Aboriginal woman has a 715 health assessment. It finds a BMI of 34 and an HbA1c of 6.2%. She wants to see a dietitian and an exercise physiologist but says she cannot afford private fees. She has no other chronic conditions and no GP management plan. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Refer her using the Medicare allied health follow-up items available after a 715 health assessment
Tell her that prediabetes does not qualify for any Medicare-funded allied health
Explain that allied health is Medicare-funded only through a GP management plan and team care arrangements
Book another 715 in 3 months to recheck her weight
Refer her to the hospital emergency department for dietetic review
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Refer her using the Medicare allied health follow-up items available after a 715 health assessment

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 715 health assessment has found a modifiable risk that needs allied health follow-up, and cost is a barrier.

2. THE RULE
Problems found at a 715 health assessment need an arranged follow-up plan, using post-assessment nurse/Aboriginal Health Practitioner and allied health follow-up items, not the next health check.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
A 715 health assessment is a starting point, not the end of care. After a 715, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients can be referred for up to 5 Medicare-funded allied health follow-up services a year (MBS items 81300 to 81360), without needing a GP management plan. Dietetics and exercise physiology are both covered.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Tell her that prediabetes does not qualify for any Medicare-funded allied health: The post-715 follow-up items are not limited to established disease. Risks identified at the assessment qualify.
C. Explain that allied health is Medicare-funded only through a GP management plan and team care arrangements: There is a separate pathway. Allied health follow-up items are available after a 715 without a GP management plan.
D. Book another 715 in 3 months to recheck her weight: A 715 is claimed no more often than every 9 months, and repeating it does not deliver the intervention she needs.
E. Refer her to the hospital emergency department for dietetic review: Emergency departments are not the pathway for planned dietetic care.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
After a 715, refer through the post-assessment allied health follow-up items (up to 5 a year).

---

items.question_text: A 715 health assessment for a 50-year-old Torres Strait Islander man shows blood pressure readings of 152/94 and 150/96 mmHg. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and wants help to quit. The GP is about to sign off the assessment and says he will look at these issues at the next health check. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Sign off the assessment. The next 715 will review the blood pressure
Start two antihypertensives today and discharge him from follow-up
Send him to the emergency department for the blood pressure
Arrange follow-up for the blood pressure and smoking, including review by the practice nurse or Aboriginal Health Practitioner under the post-715 follow-up item
Refer him urgently to a cardiologist
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Arrange follow-up for the blood pressure and smoking, including review by the practice nurse or Aboriginal Health Practitioner under the post-715 follow-up item

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 715 health assessment has found raised blood pressure and active smoking. The plan is to wait for the next health check.

2. THE RULE
Problems found at a 715 health assessment need an arranged follow-up plan, using post-assessment nurse/Aboriginal Health Practitioner and allied health follow-up items, not the next health check.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Findings from a health assessment must lead to a plan. The blood pressure needs confirmation and management, and smoking cessation support should start now. Medicare funds follow-up after a 715 by a practice nurse or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner (item 10987), alongside GP review. Waiting 9 to 12 months for the next 715 leaves the risks untreated.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Sign off the assessment. The next 715 will review the blood pressure: The 715 is not treatment. Waiting for the next check leaves raised blood pressure and smoking unmanaged.
B. Start two antihypertensives today and discharge him from follow-up: Starting dual therapy without confirming the readings, and then stopping follow-up, is unsafe.
C. Send him to the emergency department for the blood pressure: Asymptomatic raised blood pressure is not an emergency.
E. Refer him urgently to a cardiologist: Stage 2-range readings without symptoms or end-organ damage are managed in primary care, not by urgent cardiology referral.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Every abnormal 715 finding needs a follow-up plan; post-715 nurse or AHP follow-up items exist.

---

items.question_text: A 41-year-old Aboriginal woman had an MBS 715 health assessment 10 months ago. She attends as an outpatient and asks for her next one. The practice manager says another 715 cannot be claimed until 12 months have passed. What is the most appropriate response?
options: She can have the 715 now, because the minimum interval is 9 months
She must wait 2 years, as for adult health assessments
A 715 can only be claimed once in a lifetime
She must wait until 12 months have passed
She needs a specialist referral before a repeat 715
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. She can have the 715 now, because the minimum interval is 9 months

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A repeat 715 request 10 months after the last one.

2. THE RULE
The MBS 715 health assessment is offered on self-identification as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, at least 9 months apart, to a non-admitted patient, never to a hospital inpatient.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
MBS item 715 can be claimed for an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander patient no more often than once every 9 months. At 10 months she is eligible now. The patient is non-admitted, so the inpatient exclusion does not apply.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. She must wait 2 years, as for adult health assessments: There is no 2-year interval for 715.
C. A 715 can only be claimed once in a lifetime: The 715 is repeated at least 9 months apart, not once only.
D. She must wait until 12 months have passed: The interval is 9 months, not 12.
E. She needs a specialist referral before a repeat 715: No referral is needed for a 715.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A 715 can be repeated after 9 months.

---

items.question_text: A 58-year-old Torres Strait Islander man was registered for Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief by his GP in Cairns last year. He has moved to Adelaide, sees a new GP, and is told he must re-register with the new practice before the CTG benefit applies. What is the most appropriate response?
options: He loses eligibility when he leaves a remote area
He must re-register with each new practice
He must re-register every 12 months
His registration is national and one-off; he does not need to re-register
Only an Aboriginal community controlled service in Adelaide can restore it
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. His registration is national and one-off; he does not need to re-register

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A registered patient moves interstate and is told to re-register.

2. THE RULE
Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief needs a one-off registration by a PBS prescriber or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner; writing CTG on a script (optional since July 2021) or asking a pharmacist does not create eligibility.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Since 1 July 2021, CTG PBS co-payment registration is a one-off registration recorded with Services Australia and applies nationally at any pharmacy, so it continues after a move. It no longer has to be renewed with each practice or each year.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. He loses eligibility when he leaves a remote area: CTG eligibility is not limited to remote areas.
B. He must re-register with each new practice: Registration is linked to the patient, not the practice.
C. He must re-register every 12 months: There is no annual renewal.
E. Only an Aboriginal community controlled service in Adelaide can restore it: Any PBS prescriber's earlier registration stays valid.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
CTG PBS registration is one-off and national.

---

items.question_text: A 12-year-old Aboriginal girl in a remote Northern Territory community has a single hot, swollen knee and fever of 38.4°C. CRP is 90 mg/L. A sore throat 3 weeks ago was not treated. A registrar says ARF needs polyarthritis, so this is septic arthritis or a sprain. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Wait for a migratory pattern to develop before considering ARF
Treat as possible ARF: arrange echocardiography and joint assessment, notify, and add to the RHD register if confirmed
Give oral antibiotics and review in a month
Diagnose a sprain and give NSAIDs only
Exclude ARF because there is only one joint
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Treat as possible ARF: arrange echocardiography and joint assessment, notify, and add to the RHD register if confirmed

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A high-risk child with monoarthritis after an untreated sore throat.

2. THE RULE
Suspected acute rheumatic fever needs echocardiography, notification and referral to the RHD register.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Under the Australian ARF/RHD guideline, in high-risk populations monoarthritis (and polyarthralgia) counts as a major manifestation, because ARF commonly presents this way. Septic arthritis must still be excluded. The child needs echocardiography, notification and register referral if ARF is diagnosed. NSAIDs can mask the migratory pattern and are best held until the diagnosis is clear.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Wait for a migratory pattern to develop before considering ARF: Waiting for migration, especially on NSAIDs, delays diagnosis.
C. Give oral antibiotics and review in a month: Delay misses carditis and the start of secondary prophylaxis.
D. Diagnose a sprain and give NSAIDs only: A missed diagnosis of ARF or septic arthritis is the risk here.
E. Exclude ARF because there is only one joint: Monoarthritis is a major criterion in high-risk groups.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
In high-risk groups, monoarthritis can be a major criterion for ARF.

---

items.question_text: A 10-year-old Aboriginal boy has 3 weeks of jerky, involuntary movements of his arms and face, with clumsy handwriting. He has no fever, joint symptoms or murmur, and his CRP is normal. A colleague says ARF cannot be diagnosed without raised inflammatory markers. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose a tic disorder and reassure
Exclude ARF because inflammatory markers are normal
Consider Sydenham chorea as ARF: arrange echocardiography, notify, and start secondary prophylaxis if confirmed
Repeat the CRP in a month before acting
Refer to neurology only, as ARF is not relevant
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Consider Sydenham chorea as ARF: arrange echocardiography, notify, and start secondary prophylaxis if confirmed

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A high-risk child with isolated chorea and normal inflammatory markers.

2. THE RULE
Suspected acute rheumatic fever needs echocardiography, notification and referral to the RHD register.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Sydenham chorea is a major manifestation that can occur months after the streptococcal infection, often when inflammatory markers have returned to normal. Once other causes are excluded, chorea alone can establish ARF in the Australian guideline. Echocardiography is needed because subclinical carditis is common.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Diagnose a tic disorder and reassure: Chorea in a high-risk child should not be dismissed as tics.
B. Exclude ARF because inflammatory markers are normal: Normal markers are expected in late-onset chorea.
D. Repeat the CRP in a month before acting: Delay misses carditis and secondary prophylaxis.
E. Refer to neurology only, as ARF is not relevant: Chorea is an ARF manifestation; the cardiac risk must be assessed.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Sydenham chorea can establish ARF even with normal inflammatory markers.

---

items.question_text: A 45-year-old man who came to Australia as a refugee from Myanmar 4 years ago has newly diagnosed polymyalgia-like symptoms, and the rheumatologist plans prednisolone 15 mg daily for many months. His eosinophil count is normal and he has no gut symptoms. What is the most appropriate step before starting steroids?
options: Test for Strongyloides serology and treat with ivermectin if positive, or give empirical ivermectin if steroids cannot wait
Check a single stool microscopy and proceed if negative
Only screen people from remote northern Australia
Start steroids; a normal eosinophil count excludes Strongyloides
Give albendazole once and start steroids
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Test for Strongyloides serology and treat with ivermectin if positive, or give empirical ivermectin if steroids cannot wait

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A migrant from an endemic region about to start long-term steroids.

2. THE RULE
Before corticosteroids or immunosuppression in a person from a Strongyloides-endemic setting, check serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Strongyloides is endemic in South-East Asia as well as remote northern Australia. People from endemic areas should have serology (or empirical ivermectin) before steroids, because the infection can persist for decades and cause hyperinfection when immunosuppressed. Eosinophil counts and stool microscopy are insensitive.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Check a single stool microscopy and proceed if negative: Single stool microscopy has poor sensitivity.
C. Only screen people from remote northern Australia: Refugees and migrants from endemic regions are also at risk.
D. Start steroids; a normal eosinophil count excludes Strongyloides: A normal eosinophil count does not exclude chronic infection.
E. Give albendazole once and start steroids: Ivermectin, not albendazole, is the treatment of choice.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Screen or treat for Strongyloides before steroids in anyone from an endemic region.

---

items.question_text: A 60-year-old man from a remote Kimberley community has been on high-dose dexamethasone for 2 weeks for spinal cord compression from a lymphoma. He now has fever, abdominal pain, diffuse wheeze and Gram-negative bacteraemia (E. coli). He has never had Strongyloides testing. What is the most important additional diagnosis to consider and treat?
options: Lymphoma progression: start chemotherapy now
Steroid-induced asthma: increase the dexamethasone
Strongyloides hyperinfection: give ivermectin urgently and reduce steroids if possible
Simple E. coli urinary sepsis: antibiotics alone
Drug fever from dexamethasone: stop all medications
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Strongyloides hyperinfection: give ivermectin urgently and reduce steroids if possible

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A steroid-treated man from an endemic area with Gram-negative sepsis.

2. THE RULE
Before corticosteroids or immunosuppression in a person from a Strongyloides-endemic setting, check serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Gram-negative bacteraemia with respiratory and gut symptoms in a steroid-treated person from an endemic area suggests Strongyloides hyperinfection. Larvae carry gut bacteria into the blood. It is often fatal unless treated urgently with ivermectin, with infectious diseases input, alongside antibiotics and a reduction in immunosuppression where possible.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Lymphoma progression: start chemotherapy now: Chemotherapy would worsen immunosuppression before the infection is treated.
B. Steroid-induced asthma: increase the dexamethasone: More steroid worsens hyperinfection.
D. Simple E. coli urinary sepsis: antibiotics alone: Antibiotics alone miss the cause of the bacteraemia.
E. Drug fever from dexamethasone: stop all medications: Stopping all drugs, including antibiotics, is unsafe.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Gram-negative sepsis on steroids in an endemic patient: think Strongyloides hyperinfection.

---

items.question_text: A 52-year-old woman with diabetes in Darwin has had 2 weeks of IV meropenem for culture-confirmed melioidosis pneumonia. She is now afebrile and well. The team plans to discharge her with no further antibiotics. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Give 7 days of oral amoxicillin
Start oral eradication therapy with co-trimoxazole for at least 3 months
Continue IV meropenem for 6 more months
Give a single dose of benzathine penicillin
Discharge with no further antibiotics
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Start oral eradication therapy with co-trimoxazole for at least 3 months

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Melioidosis after completion of IV intensive therapy.

2. THE RULE
Suspected melioidosis in tropical northern Australia is treated with IV ceftazidime or meropenem, not standard community pneumonia antibiotics.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Melioidosis is treated in two phases: an intensive IV phase (ceftazidime or meropenem) followed by an eradication phase, usually oral co-trimoxazole for at least 3 months, to reduce relapse. Stopping after IV therapy alone carries a high relapse risk.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Give 7 days of oral amoxicillin: Amoxicillin is not an effective eradication regimen.
C. Continue IV meropenem for 6 more months: Long-term IV therapy is not needed once the intensive phase is complete.
D. Give a single dose of benzathine penicillin: Benzathine penicillin has no role in melioidosis.
E. Discharge with no further antibiotics: Omitting eradication therapy increases relapse.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Melioidosis needs IV intensive therapy, then at least 3 months of oral co-trimoxazole.

---

items.question_text: During ED registration, a 37-year-old man is asked the standard question about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander origin. He says he would rather not answer. The clerk plans to mark him as 'non-Indigenous' so the field is not blank. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Record 'not stated' and respect his choice; he can be asked again in future
Record 'Aboriginal' based on his surname
Record 'non-Indigenous' so the field is complete
Refuse registration until he answers
Ask him for proof of Aboriginality
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Record 'not stated' and respect his choice; he can be asked again in future

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A patient declines to answer the Indigenous status question.

2. THE RULE
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status is recorded from the person's own answer to the standard question, asked of every patient, and never assumed from appearance or required to be proven.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
The Indigenous status question is voluntary. If a person declines or does not answer, the response is recorded as 'not stated/inadequately described'. A status is never assumed or guessed from appearance, name or other cues, and no proof is required.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Record 'Aboriginal' based on his surname: Surnames are not a basis for Indigenous status.
C. Record 'non-Indigenous' so the field is complete: Recording a status he did not give corrupts the data.
D. Refuse registration until he answers: Care cannot be made conditional on answering.
E. Ask him for proof of Aboriginality: Proof of Aboriginality is never required for health records.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
If a person declines, record 'not stated'; never assume.

---

items.question_text: A 26-year-old Aboriginal woman with rheumatic heart disease and a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin. A home pregnancy test is positive and she is about 6 weeks pregnant. She feels well and her next cardiology review is in 4 months. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Book routine low-risk midwifery care
Switch to a direct oral anticoagulant
Stop warfarin today with no replacement
Arrange urgent specialist review (obstetric medicine and cardiology) now to plan anticoagulation
Keep her on warfarin and review at the booked cardiology visit
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Arrange urgent specialist review (obstetric medicine and cardiology) now to plan anticoagulation

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Early pregnancy in a woman with a mechanical valve on warfarin.

2. THE RULE
A pregnant woman with known RHD needs shared specialist obstetric and cardiac care and continued secondary prophylaxis, not routine low-risk care.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
A mechanical valve in pregnancy is very high risk. Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester (especially weeks 6 to 12), but stopping anticoagulation risks valve thrombosis. She needs urgent multidisciplinary specialist planning about warfarin versus LMWH, while secondary prophylaxis continues.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Book routine low-risk midwifery care: Routine low-risk care is unsafe with RHD and a mechanical valve.
B. Switch to a direct oral anticoagulant: DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves.
C. Stop warfarin today with no replacement: Stopping anticoagulation risks valve thrombosis.
E. Keep her on warfarin and review at the booked cardiology visit: Waiting 4 months passes the critical embryopathy window.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Mechanical valve plus pregnancy: urgent specialist planning, never routine care.

---

items.question_text: A 64-year-old man in a remote community has thick, crusted, scaly plaques on his hands and back with little itch. Several family members and visiting health workers now have itchy rashes. Skin scrapings show many mites. The nurse plans a single permethrin application for him and his household. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Treat as crusted scabies: repeated oral ivermectin plus topical scabicide and keratolytic, specialist input, and treatment of all contacts
A single permethrin application for him and the household
Permethrin for him alone, as contacts have only a hypersensitivity rash
Oral antibiotics only
Topical steroid for presumed psoriasis
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Treat as crusted scabies: repeated oral ivermectin plus topical scabicide and keratolytic, specialist input, and treatment of all contacts

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Crusted scabies in an older man with symptomatic contacts.

2. THE RULE
Scabies is treated in the whole household at the same time, with impetigo treated alongside, not just the index child.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Crusted scabies involves a very high mite load and is highly contagious. It needs multiple doses of oral ivermectin with topical permethrin and keratolytic therapy, usually with hospital or specialist involvement, and screening and treatment of all contacts. In the Northern Territory it is notifiable. A single permethrin application is inadequate.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. A single permethrin application for him and the household: One application of permethrin fails in crusted scabies.
C. Permethrin for him alone, as contacts have only a hypersensitivity rash: Contacts need treatment because transmission is high.
D. Oral antibiotics only: Antibiotics treat secondary infection only.
E. Topical steroid for presumed psoriasis: Steroids will worsen scabies.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Crusted scabies needs repeated ivermectin plus topical therapy and contact treatment.

---

items.question_text: A 58-year-old Aboriginal man with an infected diabetic foot wound needs IV antibiotics for a week. A close relative has just died, and he says he must return to his community for sorry business and will leave today. He has capacity. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Refuse to discuss sorry business as it is not a medical issue
Ask security to keep him on the ward
Involve the Aboriginal Liaison Officer to plan care that allows him to attend, such as early follow-up, oral or outreach therapy, with risks explained
Stop his antibiotics because he is leaving
Tell him he will be discharged against medical advice and give no plan
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Involve the Aboriginal Liaison Officer to plan care that allows him to attend, such as early follow-up, oral or outreach therapy, with risks explained

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A patient needing IV antibiotics wants to leave for sorry business.

2. THE RULE
Culturally safe care follows the patient's wishes about family and Aboriginal Health Workers but never replaces or delays clinical assessment, and symptoms are not attributed to stereotypes.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Culturally safe care recognises the importance of sorry business and works with the patient, the Aboriginal Liaison Officer and the community health service to find a safe plan, such as oral antibiotics, outreach care and a planned return, while explaining the clinical risks. A person with capacity cannot be detained.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Refuse to discuss sorry business as it is not a medical issue: Dismissing cultural obligations undermines trust and engagement.
B. Ask security to keep him on the ward: A competent adult cannot be detained to receive treatment.
D. Stop his antibiotics because he is leaving: Stopping treatment is unsafe when alternatives exist.
E. Tell him he will be discharged against medical advice and give no plan: Leaving him without a plan increases harm.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Plan care around cultural obligations with the ALO rather than forcing a choice.

---

items.question_text: A trachoma-endemic community has had azithromycin mass drug administration twice, but child prevalence remains high. Many children have dirty faces with flies around their eyes, and several houses lack working taps. The visiting team plans a third antibiotic round only. What is the most appropriate addition?
options: Stop antibiotics because they have failed
Switch to topical chloramphenicol drops for every child
Refer every child for eyelid surgery
Strengthen facial cleanliness and environmental improvement (working washing facilities) alongside antibiotics
Screen only adults for trichiasis
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Strengthen facial cleanliness and environmental improvement (working washing facilities) alongside antibiotics

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Persistent trachoma despite antibiotic rounds.

2. THE RULE
Trachoma in an endemic community is managed with the SAFE strategy (surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, environmental improvement).

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
The SAFE strategy combines Surgery for trichiasis, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness and Environmental improvement. Antibiotics alone do not stop reinfection when face washing and functioning washing facilities are lacking.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Stop antibiotics because they have failed: Antibiotics remain part of SAFE; the missing parts must be added.
B. Switch to topical chloramphenicol drops for every child: Topical drops are not the community control approach.
C. Refer every child for eyelid surgery: Surgery is for trichiasis, not active trachoma.
E. Screen only adults for trichiasis: Children are the main reservoir of active trachoma.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
SAFE needs facial cleanliness and environment, not antibiotics alone.

---

items.question_text: A 4-year-old Aboriginal boy has a 715 health assessment. His immunisation record on the AIR shows he missed his 18-month vaccines and his 4-year vaccines are due. He is well today. His parent is happy to proceed. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Note the gap and wait until the next 715 in 9 months
Refer to a paediatrician before any vaccine is given
Restart the whole childhood schedule
Tell the parent the missed 18-month vaccines can no longer be given
Give the due and catch-up vaccines today if appropriate and record a follow-up plan
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Give the due and catch-up vaccines today if appropriate and record a follow-up plan

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Missed vaccinations found at a child's 715.

2. THE RULE
Problems found at a 715 health assessment need an arranged follow-up plan, using post-assessment nurse/Aboriginal Health Practitioner and allied health follow-up items, not the next health check.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
A 715 health assessment is an opportunity to act on gaps found. Catch-up vaccination should start at the visit, using all documented doses and the minimum intervals, with the plan recorded and follow-up arranged.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Note the gap and wait until the next 715 in 9 months: Waiting for the next assessment leaves him unprotected.
B. Refer to a paediatrician before any vaccine is given: A well child does not need specialist review before catch-up.
C. Restart the whole childhood schedule: The schedule is never restarted.
D. Tell the parent the missed 18-month vaccines can no longer be given: Missed doses are caught up, not abandoned.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Gaps found at a 715 are acted on with a follow-up plan, such as catch-up vaccination.

---

items.question_text: A 6-year-old Aboriginal girl in a remote community has three crusted, purulent skin sores on her legs. She is otherwise well. The nurse plans topical mupirocin because the sores are small. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Wash with soap and review in 2 weeks
Systemic treatment: oral co-trimoxazole for 3 to 5 days, or a single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin dose
Oral amoxicillin for 1 day
Topical mupirocin
Topical steroid cream
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Systemic treatment: oral co-trimoxazole for 3 to 5 days, or a single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin dose

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Impetigo in a child in a high-risk community.

2. THE RULE
In populations at high risk of rheumatic fever, sore throats (ages 3-35) and skin sores are treated promptly as streptococcal, e.g. IM benzathine benzylpenicillin G or 10 days of amoxicillin, without waiting for swab results.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
In high-risk Aboriginal communities, impetigo (skin sores) is treated systemically, with oral co-trimoxazole for 3 to 5 days or IM benzathine benzylpenicillin, to clear Streptococcus pyogenes and reduce the risk of APSGN and probably ARF. Topical antibiotics are not recommended in this setting because of resistance and poor efficacy.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Wash with soap and review in 2 weeks: Hygiene alone does not treat streptococcal skin infection.
C. Oral amoxicillin for 1 day: A single day of amoxicillin is inadequate.
D. Topical mupirocin: Topical mupirocin is not recommended for impetigo in high-risk communities.
E. Topical steroid cream: Steroids may worsen infection.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
High-risk impetigo is treated systemically, not with topical antibiotics.

---

items.question_text: A 7-year-old boy in a remote community has had a discharging ear with a perforated drum for 3 months. The clinic plans oral amoxicillin and asks the family to keep the ear dry until the next visit in 6 weeks. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Regular ear toilet (dry mopping or syringing) followed by topical ciprofloxacin drops, with hearing assessment
Advise that the perforation will heal without treatment
Refer for grommets
Aminoglycoside ear drops
Oral amoxicillin and review in 6 weeks
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Regular ear toilet (dry mopping or syringing) followed by topical ciprofloxacin drops, with hearing assessment

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Chronic ear discharge through a perforation in a remote child.

2. THE RULE
Chronic suppurative otitis media in a remote child is actively treated with ear cleaning and topical antibiotics and the hearing is formally assessed.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
CSOM (discharge through a perforation for more than 6 weeks) is treated with frequent ear cleaning followed by topical ciprofloxacin drops, continued until the ear is dry, with follow-up and hearing assessment. Oral antibiotics alone are less effective. Ciprofloxacin is preferred because aminoglycoside drops carry a risk of ototoxicity with a perforated drum.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Advise that the perforation will heal without treatment: Untreated CSOM causes hearing loss and complications.
C. Refer for grommets: Grommets are not the treatment for an existing perforation.
D. Aminoglycoside ear drops: Aminoglycoside drops risk ototoxicity with a perforated drum.
E. Oral amoxicillin and review in 6 weeks: Oral antibiotics alone are less effective than ear toilet plus topical quinolone.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
CSOM: ear toilet plus topical ciprofloxacin, with hearing assessment.

---

items.question_text: A 32-year-old Aboriginal man attends for a health check. He smokes and his blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg. He has no known heart disease. A registrar, using the old 2012 guideline, says formal cardiovascular risk assessment starts at 35 for Aboriginal people. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Wait until he is 45, as for the general population
Wait until he is 35
Assess his cardiovascular risk now; the 2023 guideline recommends assessment from 30 years for First Nations people
Assess risk only if he has diabetes
Assess risk only after a cardiac event
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Assess his cardiovascular risk now; the 2023 guideline recommends assessment from 30 years for First Nations people

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 32-year-old Aboriginal smoker at a health check.

2. THE RULE
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults have cardiovascular risk assessed from 30 years, and standard calculators may underestimate their risk.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
The 2023 Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk recommends assessment from 30 years for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people (compared with 45 to 79 in the general population), using the Aus CVD Risk Calculator with recalibration as advised. The previous guideline started at 35.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Wait until he is 45, as for the general population: 45 applies to the general population.
B. Wait until he is 35: 35 was the previous recommendation, now replaced.
D. Assess risk only if he has diabetes: Assessment does not depend on diabetes.
E. Assess risk only after a cardiac event: Waiting for an event defeats primary prevention.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
From 2023, First Nations CVD risk assessment starts at 30.

---

items.question_text: A 44-year-old Aboriginal woman has diabetes and chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 40 mL/min/1.73 m² and persistent albuminuria. A registrar enters her details into the risk calculator, gets a moderate 5-year risk, and plans lifestyle advice alone. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Use a standard calculator without adjustment
She is at high risk on clinical criteria, so the calculator is not needed and treatment should be intensified
Rely on the calculator: moderate risk means lifestyle advice only
Cardiovascular risk cannot be assessed until she is 45
Repeat the calculator in 5 years
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. She is at high risk on clinical criteria, so the calculator is not needed and treatment should be intensified

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A First Nations woman with CKD and a moderate calculator score.

2. THE RULE
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults have cardiovascular risk assessed from 30 years, and standard calculators may underestimate their risk.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
The 2023 Australian guideline lists conditions that place people at high cardiovascular risk without calculation, including moderate to severe chronic kidney disease (such as eGFR below 45 or persistent significant albuminuria). These people need full risk-reducing treatment, including lipid and blood pressure management.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Use a standard calculator without adjustment: Standard tools underestimate First Nations risk.
C. Rely on the calculator: moderate risk means lifestyle advice only: A calculator underestimates risk in people already at high clinical risk.
D. Cardiovascular risk cannot be assessed until she is 45: First Nations assessment starts from 30.
E. Repeat the calculator in 5 years: Waiting 5 years leaves high risk untreated.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Clinically high-risk conditions such as moderate to severe CKD need no calculator.

---
